summary:
Martian Map: slope-aware route planner for Jezero Crater

Martian Map gives a future Mars explorer a layered view of Jezero Crater and a safe walking route across it. It uses the USGS Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM mosaic (20 m/pixel, built from MRO Context Camera stereo pairs). From that elevation data it computes hillshade and slope layers, which can be toggled on the interactive map.

Routes are found with an A* search where cost rises with slope and terrain steeper than 25° is blocked. The side panel summarizes each route: distance, max and mean slope, elevation gain, and estimated walking time at an assumed 2.5 km/h. The demo route is 3.53 km, about 1.4 hours, with a max slope of 4.8°. It stays on flat ground and avoids the steep rim of the nearby crater.

The tool also exports the terrain as a standard Nav2 occupancy map (steep terrain marked as obstacle), so a ROS 2 rover simulation can load it. This builds on my earlier ROS 2 Nav2 work. Connecting the two in simulation is the next step.

Limitations: the current version uses one elevation source, so adding orthoimagery and mineral maps from other missions is the next step. The DEM mosaic has a seam that produces a small artifact in the slope layer, and the 2.5 km/h walking pace is an assumption.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Martian Map is an interactive, layered map of Jezero Crater that helps plan a safe walking route for a future Mars explorer. It combines elevation, hillshade and slope layers on one map that can be toggled on and off. The user sees a route between a start and end point, plus a summary panel with distance, max and mean slope, elevation gain, and estimated walking time.

HOW IT WORKS

The tool starts from the USGS Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM mosaic (20 m/pixel), built from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Context Camera stereo pairs. A Python script crops the area of interest, computes slope and hillshade from the elevation data, and turns slope into a travel cost. A least-cost A* search then finds the route that avoids steep ground. Terrain steeper than 25 degrees is blocked entirely. The results are rendered as image layers in an interactive Leaflet web map.

Demo route: 3.53 km, about 1.4 hours at an assumed 2.5 km/h walking pace, max slope 4.8 degrees, 64 m total elevation gain. It stays on flat ground and avoids the steep rim of the nearby crater.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

An astronaut on foot cannot take a straight line across unknown terrain. This gives mission planners a fast way to see how long a Marswalk would take, how steep it gets, and which areas to avoid. The same approach works for any location covered by a DEM.

The tool also exports the terrain as a standard Nav2 occupancy map (steep terrain marked as obstacle), so the same data can be loaded into a ROS 2 rover simulation. This builds on my earlier ROS 2 Nav2 work, and connecting the two in simulation is the next step.

TOOLS

Python, rasterio, NumPy, scikit-image (route search), Matplotlib and Pillow (image layers), Leaflet.js (interactive map), GitHub Pages (hosting). Data: USGS Astrogeology Science Center, Mars 2020 Science Investigation CTX DEM Mosaic. I built this solo in about 48 hours of the event and used Claude (an AI assistant) for planning, code and debugging.

WHAT'S CREATIVE

Instead of a static map, the route is derived from terrain physics: slope is converted into effort and safety limits, so the output is something an explorer could act on. The slope-to-costmap approach also connects planetary mapping to robotics tools, via the Nav2 export.

FACTORS CONSIDERED AND LIMITS

I limited the scope to one site so the result could be done well in 48 hours. The map uses one elevation source, so adding orthoimagery and mineral maps from other missions is the next step. The DEM mosaic has a seam that creates a small artifact in the slope layer, and the 2.5 km/h walking pace is an assumption, not a measured EVA figure.

Live demo: https://sulya09.github.io/NASA-Space-Apps/

Code and data: https://github.com/Sulya09/NASA-Space-Apps
